newsitem.title: USA: Record Norfolk deal fails to cool US Treasury mkt.
newsitem.headline: Record Norfolk deal fails to cool US Treasury mkt.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries held well and continued to trade near the top of recent ranges on Wednesday, despite a record corporate bond offering that hit the Street.

Norfolk Southern Corp sold $4.3 billion of notes and bonds in what was said to be the largest investment grade offering ever. Frequently, large corporate deals weigh on Treasuries, as dealers hedge, swap and outright sell Treasuries for the new issue, which typically gives investors more bang for their dollar with a higher yield.
But traders said there was very little of that on Wednesday. Rather, the issue was bought with "real money," said a trader at one of the lead dealers.
"It was done for cash," he said. "It was not on swap. That's why there is no pressure on Treasuries."
Traders said that the deal was sold out hours before it was priced.

"The deal was oversubscribed," said another trader at a primary dealership before the deal was priced. He noted that there was selling of off-the-run Treasuries and corporate bonds by some dealers to make room for the Norfolk deal.
Craig Coats, co-head of taxable fixed income at Prudential Securities Inc, said that, if the market was nervous about the deal, players would have hedged positions.

Coats said the market did not have to hedge since investors have plenty of money that needs to be put to work, given the hefty jump in the Dow industrials over the past month, a government interest payment and maturing cash management bills.
At the time of the 1500 EDT pricing, Treasuries were higher across the board, with the 30-year bond up nearly a half-point.

Earlier, bonds had risen as much as 3/4-point on a surprising 0.6 percent fall in the overall producer price index (PPI), coupled with a 0.1 percent fall in the PPI core rate. But unsubstantiated rumors of the administration endorsing a 115 dollar-yen level took Treasuries slightly off their intraday highs.
Some traders said the market should be firmer, especially after PPI, but there are not enough shorts remaining.

"Most dealers are close to where they want to be position-wise," said Coats. "The market is not going to have a significant move until we get to next week (when the Federal Reserve's policy setting committee meets on Tuesday)."
